(2023) — Laws 2023, ch. 190 (SB 1148) added § 39-129 (local law-enforcement video fee ceiling, $46 per video-hour reviewed) and amended § 39-127; 56th Leg. 2nd Reg. (2024) — Laws 2024, ch. 56 (SB 1371) amended § 39-127; 57th Leg. 1st Reg. (2025) — Laws 2025, ch. 37 and ch. 65 (SB 1220) amended § 39-127 (audio recordings; prosecutorial agency), Laws 2025, ch. 102 (SB 1372, approved May 2, 2025) amended § 39-121.01(D)(1) to require the requester to affirm non-commercial purpose at the time of request (general effective date Sept. 26, 2025); 57th Leg. 2nd Reg. (2026, adjourned) — SB 1437 ('fee ... shall be based on material costs only', preference for electronic copies) reported dead after Senate passage (third-party status, not enacted; codified text carries no such language); HB 2139 (would add 'reasonable' fee) last action House second reading Jan. 13, 2026, not enacted; HB 4056 (new § 39-130, no fees for legislators' requests) vetoed June 19, 2026 (per press veto tracker; § 39-130 absent from azleg TOC). § 39-121.03 (commercial charge) and § 39-122 unchanged 2024–2026. Arizona has NO administrative-code or AG-rule fee schedule for public records and no rulemaking delegation in § 39-121.01; the operative non-commercial limits (copying + postage only; no search/retrieval charge) come from Hanania v. City of Tucson (App. 1980) as restated in formal Ariz. Att'y Gen. Op. I13-012 (R13-018) and the AG Agency Handbook ch. 6 § 6.5.5, and Ombudsman-Citizens' Aide guidance adds a broader no-labor/no-redaction/no-overhead gloss. Guidance-vs-law gap: the AG handbook allows 'a reasonable amount for the cost of time, equipment, and personnel used in producing copies' while the Ombudsman FAQ says no charge for 'labor'; neither is statute. AG Op. I86-090 not openable on azag.gov.

resolutions.source_language: The custodian of such records shall promptly furnish such copies, printouts or photographs and may charge a fee if the facilities are available, except that public records for purposes listed in section 39-122 or 39-127 shall be furnished without charge.

resolutions.manual_verification: Statute sets no rate and no express standard; the copying-cost limitation comes from case law (Hanania) as restated in a formal AG opinion and the AG handbook, not from statute text.
resolutions.notes: Statute is a bare Permission ('may charge a fee if the facilities are available') with no per-page number and no rulemaking delegation; the custodian (for a city, the city) sets the rate. AG guidance frames the permissible non-commercial fee as one that offsets copying costs, 'including a reasonable amount for the cost of time, equipment, and personnel used in producing copies of records, but not for costs of searching for the records' (AZ-9004). No graduated bands, no free pages. 2026 SB 1437 ('material costs only') and HB 2139 ('reasonable fee') were not enacted.

resolutions.source_language: In Hanania v. City of Tucson, 128 Ariz. 135, 136, 624 P.2d 332, 333 (App. 1981), the court determined that the public records law allowed a public body to charge a fee for copying a public record, but not for searching for or retrieving the record. This plain language indicates that a public body may charge a fee for responding to a public records request for a noncommercial purpose for (1) postage charges to mail copies of public records to the requesting party or (2) copying public records and furnishing them to the requesting party if the proper facilities are available.
resolutions.effective_status: Current (opinion dated Dec. 2, 2013; § 39-121.01(D)(1) fee sentence unchanged through Laws 2025, ch. 102)
resolutions.manual_verification: The categorical bar is judicial/AG-opinion law, not statute text; AG Op. I86-090 could not be opened on azag.gov (only cited through I13-012 and the AG handbook).
resolutions.notes: For NON-commercial requests a search/retrieval labor rate cannot exist: the fee is limited to copying and postage. For COMMERCIAL requests § 39-121.03(A)(2) permits 'a reasonable fee for the cost of time, materials, equipment and personnel in producing such reproduction' (AZ-0019, see item commercial). Local law-enforcement video: review time is folded into the § 39-129 per-video-hour ceiling (item av).

resolutions.source_authority: Ariz. Att'y Gen. Op. I13-012 (R13-018); Arizona Ombudsman-Citizens' Aide, Public Records FAQ ('Can the public body charge me for copies?')
resolutions.source_language: This plain language indicates that a public body may charge a fee for responding to a public records request for a noncommercial purpose for (1) postage charges to mail copies of public records to the requesting party or (2) copying public records and furnishing them to the requesting party if the proper facilities are available. [Ombudsman FAQ:] The public body may not charge for the cost of searching the records. Hanania v. City of Tucson, 128 Ariz. 135, 624 P.2d 332 (Ct. App. 1980); Ariz. Att'y Gen. Op. I13-012. The public body also cannot charge for inspection of the record, labor, redaction, overhead costs, or any fee to examine or review a record to determine whether the record is disclosable.
resolutions.effective_status: Current (AG opinion 2013; Ombudsman FAQ opened 2026-08-19)
resolutions.manual_verification: The explicit 'cannot charge for ... redaction ... or any fee to examine or review a record to determine whether the record is disclosable' sentence is Ombudsman guidance (lowest tier); the AG opinion states the general copying-and-postage-only rule and the inspection-context redaction bar. Human legal review before configuring any redaction labor line for a non-commercial request.
resolutions.notes: Non-commercial: review/redaction labor is not a chargeable component (fee limited to copying and postage). Exceptions: commercial requests (§ 39-121.03(A)(2)); local law-enforcement video recordings, where 'the reasonable cost of reviewing ... and, as necessary, redacting the video recording' may be considered inside the $46/video-hour onetime-fee ceiling (§ 39-129, AZ-9001).

new_rules.legal_concept: Non-commercial fee limited to copying and postage; no charge for searching for or retrieving records (Hanania rule)
new_rules.atomic_rule: For a non-commercial request a public body may charge only (1) postage to mail copies and (2) the cost of copying records it furnishes; it may not charge for searching for or retrieving the record.
new_rules.trigger: Request is not for a commercial purpose (§ 39-121.03).
new_rules.source_language: This plain language indicates that a public body may charge a fee for responding to a public records request for a noncommercial purpose for (1) postage charges to mail copies of public records to the requesting party or (2) copying public records and furnishing them to the requesting party if the proper facilities are available. In Hanania v. City of Tucson, 128 Ariz. 135, 136, 624 P.2d 332, 333 (App. 1981), the court determined that the public records law allowed a public body to charge a fee for copying a public record, but not for searching for or retrieving the record. Arizona's public records law allows a public body to impose copying fees in response to public records requests for noncommercial purposes. Under that law, a public body can impose copying fees to offset copying costs only when a requesting party asks the public body to furnish copies of records. A public body should not impose copying fees on a party making a public records request when the requesting party asks only to inspect records or uses a personal device to make his or her own copies.
new_rules.source_authority: Ariz. Att'y Gen. Op. I13-012 (R13-018), Dec. 2, 2013 (restating Hanania v. City of Tucson, 128 Ariz. 135 (App. 1980) and Ariz. Att'y Gen. Op. I86-090)
new_rules.effective_status: Current (opinion 2013; underlying § 39-121.01(D)(1) fee sentence unchanged through Laws 2025, ch. 102)

new_rules.legal_concept: No copying fee for inspection-only requests or personal-device copies
new_rules.atomic_rule: A public body may not charge a copying fee when the requester asks only to inspect records (even if the body must print or copy internally, e.g., to redact) or when the requester makes copies with a personal device.
new_rules.trigger: Requester asks to inspect only, or copies with own device (non-disruptive).
new_rules.source_language: A public body in Arizona therefore cannot charge copying fees to recoup the cost of copies made internally to allow a member of the public to inspect the records. ... For these reasons, a public body cannot charge a copying fee when a member of the public inspects a record and makes a copy of the record using his or her own personal device.

new_rules.legal_concept: Permissible non-commercial copying fee: amount the agency deems appropriate for copying, including a reasonable amount for time, equipment and personnel used in producing copies — not search costs
new_rules.atomic_rule: An agency may charge a fee it deems appropriate for copying records, including a reasonable amount for the cost of time, equipment and personnel used in producing copies, but not for costs of searching for the records.
new_rules.source_language: An agency may charge a fee it deems appropriate for copying records, including a reasonable amount for the cost of time, equipment, and personnel used in producing copies of records, but not for costs of searching for the records. A.R.S. § 39-121.01(D)(1); Hanania v. City of Tucson, 128 Ariz. 135, 136, 624 P.2d 332, 333 (App. 1980); Ariz. Att'y Gen. Op. I86-090. When the requester only wants to inspect the record, the agency may not charge a copying fee incurred, for example, to make redactions before public inspection. Ariz. Att'y Gen. Op. I13-012.
new_rules.source_authority: Arizona Attorney General, Agency Handbook, ch. 6 (Public Records) § 6.5.5 (rev. 2018; corrected copy posted azag.gov May 2025)
new_rules.effective_status: Current (rev. 2018 handbook; posted 2025-05; reproduced in Ombudsman 2025 booklet)
new_rules.notes: Guidance, not law: it glosses § 39-121.01(D)(1) via Hanania and AG Op. I86-090. Written for state agencies but states the § 39-121.01 rule that applies to all public bodies. Note tension with the Ombudsman FAQ (AZ-9005), which lists 'labor' among non-chargeable items; the handbook admits copy-production personnel time. Constraint basis soft-standard: no number.

new_rules.legal_concept: Ombudsman guidance: no charge for inspection, labor, redaction, overhead, or review to determine disclosability
new_rules.atomic_rule: The public body cannot charge for the cost of searching, for inspection of the record, labor, redaction, overhead costs, or any fee to examine or review a record to determine whether it is disclosable.
new_rules.source_language: The public body may not charge for the cost of searching the records. Hanania v. City of Tucson, 128 Ariz. 135, 624 P.2d 332 (Ct. App. 1980); Ariz. Att'y Gen. Op. I13-012. The public body also cannot charge for inspection of the record, labor, redaction, overhead costs, or any fee to examine or review a record to determine whether the record is disclosable.
new_rules.source_authority: Arizona Ombudsman-Citizens' Aide, FAQs – Public Records ('Can the public body charge me for copies?')
new_rules.notes: Lowest tier of the source hierarchy (records-authority FAQ). Broader than the AG opinion it cites (adds redaction/overhead/review). Human legal review before treating the redaction/overhead bar as binding; § 39-129 expressly lets local LE video fees consider review/redaction cost within its cap.

new_rules.legal_concept: Fee waiver is discretionary; no hardship waiver required
new_rules.atomic_rule: A public body is not required to waive a copying fee for financial hardship, but is not required to impose a charge for copies at all.
new_rules.trigger: Requester asks for a fee waiver (non-statutory ground).
new_rules.source_language: I requested copies of public records and cannot afford the copying fee. Must the public body waive the copying fee if it causes financial hardship? No. The law permits public bodies to impose a copying fee and does not require a waiver for financial hardship. That said, public bodies are not required to impose a charge for copies.
new_rules.source_authority: Arizona Ombudsman-Citizens' Aide, FAQs – Public Records
new_rules.notes: Guidance only; statute is silent on discretionary waivers. Mandatory no-charge categories are § 39-122 and § 39-127 (AZ-9008, AZ-9009).

new_rules.legal_concept: Requester must affirm non-commercial purpose (or undertake to give a commercial-purpose statement) at the time of the request
new_rules.atomic_rule: At the time of the request the requesting person shall affirm that the record is not for a commercial purpose or, if it is, that the person will provide the § 39-121.03(A) statement of intended use.
new_rules.trigger: Any request to examine or be furnished copies.
new_rules.source_language: At the time of the request, the requesting person shall affirm that the public record is not for a commercial purpose or, if the public record is for a commercial purpose, that the requesting person will provide a statement that explains the intended use pursuant to section 39-121.03, subsection A.

new_rules.legal_concept: No fee for certified copies of, or searches for, public records used in claims/benefits presented to the United States (verbatim replacement for AZ-0020)
new_rules.atomic_rule: No state, county or city (or officer or board thereof) shall demand or receive a fee for issuing certified copies of public records or for making search for them when they are to be used in connection with a claim for a pension, allotment, allowance, compensation, insurance or other benefits presented to the United States; the service is rendered on request of a US official, the claimant, or the claimant's guardian or attorney.
new_rules.trigger: Records to be used with a claim/benefit presented to the United States; request by US official, claimant, guardian or attorney.
new_rules.source_language: A. No state, county or city, or any officer or board thereof shall demand or receive a fee or compensation for issuing certified copies of public records or for making search for them, when they are to be used in connection with a claim for a pension, allotment, allowance, compensation, insurance or other benefits which is to be presented to the United States or a bureau or department thereof. C. The services specified in subsections A and B shall be rendered on request of an official of the United States, a claimant, his guardian or attorney. For each failure or refusal so to do, the officer so failing shall be liable on his official bond.
new_rules.notes: AMENDS AZ-0020 (which carried is_paraphrase=true): supplies the verbatim clause. Applies to 'state, county or city' — all public bodies. Search AND certified-copy fees both barred.

new_rules.legal_concept: Crime victims: one free copy of police report, audio recordings and video recordings (verbatim replacement for AZ-0021; reflects 2024–2025 amendments)
new_rules.atomic_rule: A victim of a Part I crime (or delinquent act), the victim's attorney, or an immediate family member if the victim is killed or incapacitated has the right to receive one copy of the police report, audio recordings and video recordings from the investigating law enforcement agency or charging prosecutorial agency at no charge; DV/sexual-offense victims have the same right regardless of Part I status; law-enforcement agencies shall prioritize processing such requests.
new_rules.trigger: Requester qualifies as victim/attorney/immediate family under § 39-127(A)–(C) and requests the police report / recordings of that offense.
new_rules.source_language: A. A victim of a criminal offense that is a part I crime under the statewide uniform crime reporting program, the victim's attorney on behalf of the victim or an immediate family member of the victim if the victim is killed or incapacitated has the right to receive one copy of the police report, audio recordings and video recordings from the investigating law enforcement agency or charging prosecutorial agency at no charge and, on request of the victim, the court or the clerk of the court shall provide, at no charge, the minute entry or portion of the record of any proceeding in the case that arises out of the offense committed against the victim and that is reasonably necessary to pursue a claimed victim's right. C. Notwithstanding subsection A or B of this section, if a police report involves a domestic violence offense or a sexual offense, the victim or the victim's attorney on behalf of the victim has the right to receive one copy of the police report, audio recordings and video recordings from the investigating law enforcement agency or charging prosecutorial agency at no charge and, on request of the victim, the court or the clerk of the court shall provide, at no charge, the minute entry or portion of the record of any proceeding in the case that arises out of the offense committed against the victim and that is reasonably necessary to pursue a claimed victim's right. D. A law enforcement agency shall prioritize the processing and providing of each police report that is requested pursuant to this section.

applicability_notes: § 39-121.01 defines 'public body' to include this state, any county, city, town, school district and political subdivision — every fee row from § 39-121.01 / § 39-121.03 / § 39-122 is all_public_bodies (single regime; Arizona does not run separate agency vs local fee regimes for records).

§ 39-129 ($46 per video-hour reviewed) is expressly limited to 'a county, a city, a town or any political subdivision of this state' charging for local law-enforcement video — recorded as applies_to=municipalities; state agencies (e.g., DPS) are outside it.

§ 41-126(A) sets the Secretary of State's own copy (no more than ten cents per page) and certification (no more than three dollars) caps — agency-specific, does not bind municipalities; not extracted as a rule row (out of municipal scope) but noted so it is not mistaken for a statewide schedule.

A.R.S. § 9-499.15 (60-day website notice before a municipality adopts a new or increased fee 'on a business') was reviewed; its applicability to a general public-records copy schedule is unclear (subsection A is framed around fees on a business) — not encoded; flagged for the city's counsel.
AG Agency Handbook ch. 6 is written for state agencies but restates § 39-121.01 rules that apply to all public bodies; treated as guidance for cities, not as an agency-only schedule.
§ 39-127 free copies bind 'the investigating law enforcement agency or charging prosecutorial agency' — for a city, its police department and city prosecutor.
material_negatives: No statewide per-page copy rate, no graduated bands, no free-page allowance, no minimum or de-minimis fee, no request-level dollar cap for municipalities (statute: bare 'may charge a fee').
No fee-estimate, cost-notice, estimate-response window, revision or validity rule; no deposit threshold or percentage cap; no nonpayment-withdrawal clock; no electronic-payment provision.
No administrative rule, AG rule or uniform fee schedule governs municipal public-records fees; § 39-121.01 contains no rulemaking delegation.

No labor charge of any kind is authorized for non-commercial requests (search/retrieval barred by Hanania/AG Op. I13-012; redaction/overhead/review barred in Ombudsman guidance) — so labor rate, increment, overhead and free-hours items are moot on the non-commercial branch.
No certified-copy fee for municipalities (only the § 39-122 no-charge rule; SOS § 41-126 is agency-only).
No fee forfeiture on late response; no repeat/aggregation rule.
